ru: Он купи́л ей пода́рок на день рожде́ния.

en_alt: Little children are happy with any presents.
Small children are pleased with any presents.
note: «ра́доваться» maps onto several equally good English verbs; the alternatives stop the word-bank drill rejecting them.

en_alt: He propped up his chin with his hand.
note: «руко́й» is instrumental, so the with-variant is the more literal reading and equally natural.

en_alt: Old things lie in the basement.
The old things are lying in the basement.
note: Russian has no article and «лежа́т» is literally 'lie', so both renderings are valid.

en_alt: The preparation for the exam took a month.
note: Article choice is free here; both readings are natural English.

ru: Мы потра́тили мно́го вре́мени на подгото́вку.

note: Terse but idiomatic Russian; the English tracks it word for word.

en_alt: He needs his friends' support.
note: The genitive «друзе́й» renders equally well as an English possessive.

en_alt: The police had a suspicion.
A suspicion arose in the police.
note: «возни́кло» is 'arose'; the alternatives keep the noun while sounding less clinical than 'developed'.

en_alt: His gaze is full of suspicion.
note: «взгляд» is 'gaze' as readily as 'look'.

ru: Её арестова́ли по подозре́нию в кра́же.

en_alt: Sign at the bottom of the page.
note: 'Put your signature' is the literal reading and stays as en_gb; the shorter form is what a native would usually write.

ru: Он объясни́л план во всех подро́бностях.
en: He explained the plan in every detail.
en_alt: He explained the plan in full detail.
note: 'in all the details' is not an English collocation; 'in every detail' renders «во всех подро́бностях» naturally.

ru: Она́ обожа́ет ходи́ть по магази́нам с подру́гами.

en_alt: My friend lives next door.
My friend lives close by.
note: «ря́дом» covers both 'nearby' and 'next door'.

ru: Пе́ред сва́дьбой она́ разосла́ла подру́гам приглаше́ния.
en_alt: Before the wedding she sent out invitations to her friends.
note: «разосла́ла» is 'sent out' (to many); the alternative catches the prefix.
The bare dative «подру́ге» idiomatically implies the speaker's own friend, so 'My friend' is not invented detail.

en_alt: Our building has four entrances.
There are four entrances in our house.
note: «дом» is house or block of flats; both word orders are natural.

en_alt: The light in the entrance is not working.
note: Progressive is the more usual English for a broken light; both track the Russian.

ru: В ночны́х поезда́х лу́чше спать на ни́жней по́лке.
en_alt: On night trains it is better to sleep on the lower berth.
note: «по́лка» in a sleeper is 'berth' as well as 'bunk'.

en_alt: The train is going to Moscow.
note: «идёт» is determinate motion, so the progressive is equally correct.

en_alt: We are going by train.
note: «е́хать» is 'go (by transport)' as much as 'travel'.

en_alt: The trip to the village was cheerful.
note: «весёлый» is literally 'cheerful'; 'fun' is the idiomatic reading and stays as en_gb.

ru: Я ча́сто вспомина́ю о той пое́здке.
en_alt: I often think back on that trip.
note: «вспомина́ть» is 'remember/recall', not 'think about'; the literal verb is just as natural here.

en_alt: The firefighters were putting out the fire all night.
note: «туши́ли» is imperfective 'were putting out'; the alternative carries the aspect explicitly.

en_alt: Yoga teaches different poses.
note: «ра́зный» is literally 'different'.

en_alt: He sat in a comfortable position.
He was sitting in a comfortable pose.
note: English usually says 'position' for a seated «по́за»; en_gb keeps the headword gloss.

en: The artist asked for the pose to be changed.
en_alt: The artist asked that the pose be changed.
note: The Russian names no addressee; the old English invented 'her'.

en_alt: The troops occupied convenient positions.
note: «заня́ть» is literally 'occupy'; both are natural military English.

en_alt: The search for work took a month.
The search for a job took a month.
note: «по́иск рабо́ты» is literally 'the search for work'; the compound noun stays as en_gb.

en_alt: The rescuers called off the search.
note: 'Called off' is the usual English for «прекрати́ли по́иски»; the literal reading stays as en_gb.

en_alt: The singer has a lot of admirers.
note: «мно́го» is 'a lot of' as readily as 'many'.

en_alt: The tractor is driving across the field.
note: «е́дет» is specifically motion by vehicle, which 'driving' catches better than 'moving'.

ru: Ра́нним у́тром тума́н сте́лется по поля́м.

en_alt: Beyond the village a field begins.
The field begins beyond the village.
note: The Russian fronts the adverbial; both English orders are valid.

en_alt: Wheat ripens in the boundless fields.
note: English normally says wheat ripens 'in' fields; «на» keeps the on-reading as en_gb.

en_alt: A famous politician made a speech.
A well-known politician made a speech.
note: «изве́стный» is 'famous'; 'gave/made a speech' are interchangeable.

en_alt: The journalists asked a question of the politician.
note: Both English objects orders render the dative «поли́тику».

en_alt: People do not believe politicians.
note: «ве́рить» + dative covers both 'trust' and 'believe'.

en_alt: Politics is a complex subject.
Politics is a complicated topic.
note: «сло́жная» is literally 'complex'.

ru: Мы спо́рили о поли́тике весь ве́чер.

en_alt: I asked the policeman the way.
note: «доро́гу» is literally 'the way'; both are idiomatic.

en_alt: The witnesses are helping the police find the car.
note: Plural «полице́йским» is naturally 'the police' in English too.

en_alt: The regiment set out for the front.
note: 'Set out' and 'set off' both render «отпра́вился».

en_alt: There are many shelves in the wardrobe.
note: «шкаф» is a cupboard or a wardrobe depending on context.

en_alt: The books stand on the shelf.
note: «стоя́т» is literally 'stand', which is natural English for books.

en_alt: The soldiers listened to the order of the colonel.
note: The genitive renders either way in English.
'Provisions' is the correct legal sense of «положе́ния», but the headword gloss is only 'position' — the gloss may be the half that needs widening.

en_alt: The cat is lying in a strip of sunlight.
note: English idiom for a band of light is 'strip'/'patch'; en_gb keeps the headword gloss 'stripe'.

en_alt: A red stripe goes along the wall.
note: «идёт» is literally 'goes'; 'runs' is the idiomatic choice.

en_alt: Obtaining the visa took a week.
Getting the visa took a week.
note: «получе́ние» as a verbal noun renders several ways; all are natural.

en_alt: Sign on receipt of the parcel.
note: 'On receipt' is the commoner English form of the same phrase.

en_alt: After receiving the letter he called.
note: The gerund reads more naturally than the nominal 'after receipt'; en_gb keeps the noun for the gloss.

ru: Э́тот сове́т пошёл мне на по́льзу.
en_alt: This advice did me good.
note: «пойти́ на по́льзу» is the fixed idiom 'to do someone good'; the noun-based en_gb keeps the headword visible.

en_alt: They act for the common good.
note: 'The common good' is the set English phrase for «о́бщая по́льза».

en_alt: Sport is of great benefit.
There is much benefit from sport.
note: The impersonal Russian construction has several natural English renderings.

en_alt: I like salad made of tomatoes.
I love tomato salad.
note: 'A salad of tomatoes' is not an English collocation; «сала́т из» is normally rendered by an attributive noun.

en_alt: A large tomato ripened in the vegetable garden.
note: «огоро́д» is specifically a vegetable garden, not an ornamental one.

ru: Я пришла́ к тебе́ за по́мощью.

en_alt: They are in need of help.
note: «нужда́ться» is closer to 'be in need of' than to plain 'need'.

en_alt: Thank you for your help.
Thanks for the help.
note: Article/possessive choice is free; the alternatives stop the drill rejecting them.

en_alt: I ask for help.
note: Russian present covers both simple and progressive English.

en_alt: I count on help.
note: Russian present covers both simple and progressive English.

ru: Нам не хвата́ет понима́ния друг дру́га.
en_alt: We lack an understanding of each other.
note: Article choice is free in English here.

ru: Он отнёсся к пробле́ме с понима́нием.
en_alt: He approached the problem with understanding.
note: «отнести́сь к» is 'take/approach an attitude towards'; both English verbs fit.

en_alt: The children are learning the basic concepts of mathematics.
note: Imperfective «у́чат» reads equally as an English progressive.

ru: Я не име́ю поня́тия об э́том.
note: «не име́ть поня́тия» is a fixed idiom and 'have no idea' is its exact English counterpart.

en_alt: Young people often listen to pop music.
note: English usually needs 'music' after 'pop' as an object.

ru: В по́пе просты́е и весёлые мело́дии.
note: «в по́пе» is both an odd way to say 'in pop music' and homophonous with the vulgar «в по́пе» ('in the bottom') — a human should decide whether to reword it as «В поп-му́зыке…».

ru: В кино́ мы взя́ли большо́й попко́рн.
en_alt: At the cinema we took a large popcorn.
At the cinema we got a big popcorn.
note: «взя́ли» is literally 'took' and «большо́й» is 'big'.

en_alt: Without popcorn the film is not the same.
note: Uncontracted form for the word-bank drill.

en_alt: The popcorn smells delicious.
The popcorn smells really good.
note: 'Smells very tasty' is a shade off in English; the alternatives are what a native would say.

en_alt: The parrot knows how to talk.
The parrot can speak.
note: «уме́ть» is 'know how to', a learned ability rather than «мочь».

en_alt: Two parrots sit in the cage.
note: Russian present covers both simple and progressive English.

ru: До сих пор я его́ не ви́дел.
en_alt: Until now I have not seen him.
So far I have not seen him.
note: «до сих пор» is a fixed phrase with several standard English equivalents.

en: In early springtime the gardens bloom.
en_alt: In the early days of spring the gardens bloom.
note: 'the early spring time' is not an English phrase; 'springtime' is the natural rendering and still carries «пора́».

en_alt: The time has come to gather in the harvest.
It is time to gather the harvest.
note: «наста́ла пора́» renders both ways in natural English.

ru: До той поры́ мы не встреча́лись.
en_alt: Until then we had not met.
note: «до той поры́» is commonly just 'until then'; the literal reading stays as en_gb.

ru: Не сто́й в дверя́х, переступи́ поро́г.

en_alt: She stopped in the doorway.
note: «на поро́ге» is often just 'in the doorway' in English; the literal reading stays as en_gb.

en_alt: An old portrait is hanging on the wall.
note: Russian present covers both simple and progressive English.

en_alt: The artist was working on the portrait.
note: «рабо́тал» is imperfective, so the progressive is the closer aspectual match.

en_alt: He left his briefcase at home.
note: 'Left ... at home' is the idiomatic English for «забы́л ... до́ма»; the literal 'forgot' stays as en_gb.

en_alt: The pupil opened his schoolbag.
note: A pupil's «портфе́ль» is a satchel/schoolbag; en_gb keeps the headword gloss.

en: The room needs to be put in order.
en_alt: Order needs to be restored in the room.
The room needs tidying up.
note: 'Order needs to be put in the room' is not English; «навести́ поря́док» is 'put in order / tidy up'.

en_alt: There is always perfect order on the table.
note: «стол» is table as well as desk.

en_alt: The museum visitor was examining the pictures.
note: «рассма́тривать» is 'examine/study closely' and «карти́ны» is 'pictures'.

en_alt: The administrator came up to the visitor.
note: «подошёл» is literally 'came up to'; «администра́тор» is also 'administrator'.

en_alt: The sick man is lying in bed.
The invalid is lying in bed.
note: «больно́й» as a noun is 'the sick person/patient'.

ru: По́сле боле́зни он лежи́т в посте́ли.
en_alt: After the illness he is lying in bed.
note: The Russian has no possessive; the article reading is equally valid.

en_alt: I like the smell of clean bedding.
I like the smell of clean sheets.
note: «посте́ль» here is the bedding rather than the bedstead.

en_alt: One must answer for one's actions.
You have to answer for your actions.
note: English idiom is 'answer for one's actions'; en_gb keeps the headword gloss 'act'.

en_alt: We talked about what he had done.
We spoke about his action.
note: 'His act' is thin English; the alternatives read naturally while en_gb keeps the gloss.

en_alt: Sweat was running down his face.
Sweat flowed down his face.
note: «тёк» is imperfective 'was flowing'.

en_alt: The shirt was soaked through with sweat.
note: «промо́кла» carries the 'through' of the prefix.

en_alt: He was taking the loss of his friend hard.
note: «пережива́л» is imperfective; the progressive matches the aspect more closely.

en_alt: The company suffered heavy losses.
The company suffered big losses.
note: 'Heavy losses' is the usual English collocation for «больши́е поте́ри».

en_alt: Losing the keys spoiled the day.
The loss of the keys ruined the day.
note: «испо́ртила» is 'spoiled/ruined'; the gerund is the commoner English.
